title: massive megalithic tombs persisted into the bronze age in spain
dek: Two monumental tombs at Trafalgar continued use well into the 2nd millennium BC.
body: Archaeologists working on the southern coast of Spain have uncovered a necropolis that rewrites the timeline of Iberian prehistory. At Trafalgar, near the Strait of Gibraltar, two monumental tombs held the remains of multiple individuals. The discovery challenges the long-held view that large collective tombs disappeared from the region at the start of the Bronze Age.

Radiocarbon dating published in PLOS One places the active use of both tombs between roughly 1875 and 1625 BC. This dates the site well after the main period associated with earlier Iberian megalithic traditions. The findings come from a team at the University of Cádiz and collaborating institutions who obtained dates from 16 individuals buried within the two structures.

During the Bronze Age, funerary customs across much of Iberia shifted dramatically. Large communal tombs were increasingly replaced by smaller structures for individuals or restricted groups. Trafalgar shows this transition was not uniform. The site remained active during the first half of the 2nd millennium BC, considerably later than the main period of Iberian megalithic burial.

One of the most striking aspects of the discovery is what the tombs lack. So far, archaeologists have found no evidence for earlier occupation or burials associated with the monuments. This absence suggests the necropolis may have been established only shortly before the dated burials, during the early 2nd millennium BC. If confirmed, it would mean communities were constructing new monumental burial spaces at a time when such traditions had largely disappeared elsewhere.

The location of the cemetery appears to have played an important role. Researchers describe Trafalgar as a new funerary space established within a landscape strongly defined by the sea. The two known tombs contained multiple individuals, maintaining a collective funerary practice with much deeper roots in Iberian prehistory. The absence of earlier archaeological material around the necropolis supports the possibility that the burial landscape was created during the Bronze Age rather than inherited from a much earlier community.

Further dating will be needed to establish when the monuments themselves were built. Strong winds and shifting sands in the coastal zone constantly change the landscape, meaning exposed archaeological remains could once again be buried under the dunes. Conservation work and further excavation will therefore be needed to determine exactly how extensive the necropolis is. More monuments could be waiting to be found around Trafalgar.

If future research supports the tombs were built in the early 2nd millennium BC, it would show that monumental collective tomb building survived in southern Iberia much later than previously thought. Instead of simply recycling monuments left behind by Copper Age communities, Bronze Age populations were still making new megalithic burial landscapes of their own. The site stands as a testament to how local traditions can persist despite broader cultural shifts.
doesnt_show: The study does not yet establish when the tombs were originally constructed, only when they were in use.
settle: Precise dating of the tomb construction phases would settle whether they were built or reused in the Bronze Age.
